title: I have sinned (2 Samuel 12:13)
hook: David answers in two Hebrew words, with no excuse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan's ewe lamb, and the line that turned the story into a mirror. Your line was the judge has written his own verdict. Today, the king answers.
screen: `THE JUDGE HAS WRITTEN HIS OWN VERDICT.`

segments.voice: Nathan has just finished speaking. The room is quiet. A king who has had a man killed now stands accused, in his own palace, by someone with no army behind him. There are plenty of things a king could say next. He could call the guards. He could explain the pressures of war, or point out that Uriah died in battle, which, on paper, is true. He could ask who else knows. The text gives him none of those lines. It gives him one short answer.
screen: `THE ROOM GOES QUIET.` → `A KING COULD SAY MANY THINGS.` → `HE SAYS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "I have sinned against the LORD." In Hebrew it's two words, chatati l'Adonai. No because. No but. Hear it next to another king. In the first book of Samuel, Saul is confronted by the prophet Samuel after he disobeys a command. Saul also says I have sinned, and then keeps going: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. The reason does some of the work of an excuse. David's sentence stops where it starts. Nathan's reply comes just as fast: the Lord has put away your sin; you shall not die. That doesn't mean nothing follows. The next words say the child born to David will die, and the chapters ahead are full of trouble in his house. Forgiveness here is real, and so are the consequences, and the text doesn't flatten either. Jewish tradition calls this kind of turning teshuvah, returning. The heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this moment, when Nathan came to David, and some readers hear it as the long version of these two words. What makes the short answer matter isn't that David feels bad. A person can feel bad and still explain. He stops defending himself. He names what he did and lets it stand. He wronged Uriah, and Bathsheba, and the people he commanded, yet he says, against the Lord. Some hear that as the deepest admission: every wrong to a person is also a wrong before God. The sentence is short. It is not small.
screen: `TWO WORDS IN HEBREW. NO BECAUSE.` · `SAUL SAID IT, THEN EXPLAINED.` · then, large: `I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.` · then: `FORGIVEN, AND STILL CONSEQUENCES.` · `PSALM 51 LOOKS BACK HERE.`

segments.voice: Let one recent thing come to mind where you got it wrong, a sharp word, a broken promise, a corner cut, and say it to yourself in one plain sentence: I did this. Notice the urge to add because, and let the because go, so the sentence stands on its own. If you pray, you can bring it before God the same way.
Chatati. The two Hebrew words David said to Nathan, meaning I have sinned, with no excuse attached. Today's word.
Your line: no because, no but. Just the plain truth, left standing. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews speak of teshuvah, returning, as naming a wrong, regretting it, and changing course; David's answer to Nathan can be read alongside Psalm 51, which its heading links to this moment.

The Hebrew is חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה, two words, as the outline's hook says; please confirm. The transliteration l'Adonai follows the custom of reading the divine name as Adonai.
Saul's confession with its reason paraphrases 1 Samuel 15:24.
